lock.title: How Mutex::lock works
lock.description: Gives one thread at a time access to the data inside.

slides.caption: lock() waits until no other thread holds the lock, then lends the data. The lock is released when the guard is dropped.
A locks, adds 1, and unlocks.
B was waiting; now it locks and adds 1.
C does the same. No update is lost.
lock() returns a Result because a thread that panicked while holding the lock "poisons" it.

channel.title: How mpsc::channel works
channel.description: Creates a channel: a Sender for one side and a Receiver for the other.

slides.caption: Values sent into tx come out of rx, in the same order.
tx sends 5 into the channel.
rx receives it.
mpsc means many producers, one consumer: clone tx to send from several threads.

send.title: How Sender::send works
send.description: Puts a value into the channel; it moves to the receiving side.

slides.caption: send never waits for the receiver (the channel has room for any number of values).
"a" is sent and now belongs to the channel.
"b" is sent from another thread through a cloned Sender.
send returns Err if the Receiver no longer exists.

recv.title: How Receiver::recv works
recv.description: Waits for the next value; Err once every Sender is gone.

slides.caption: recv blocks until a value arrives.
1 arrives.
2 arrives.
All Senders were dropped and the channel is empty: Err, and the loop ends.
for x in rx { ... } does the same thing. try_recv() never waits.

new.title: How Mutex::new works
new.description: Wraps data so only one thread at a time can use it.

slides.caption: The data lives inside the Mutex; the only way in is lock().
0 goes inside.
It starts unlocked.
Share it between threads with Arc<Mutex<T>>.

try_lock.title: How Mutex::try_lock works
try_lock.description: Locks if free right now; never waits.

slides.caption: lock() waits; try_lock() gives up at once if someone else holds the lock.
Free: you get the guard.
Held elsewhere: Err.
Useful to avoid deadlocks, or to skip work when a resource is busy.

into_inner.title: How Mutex::into_inner works
into_inner.description: Takes the data out of the Mutex for good.

slides.caption: Owning the Mutex means no other thread can use it, so no locking is needed.
The Mutex is consumed.
The Vec comes out.
With Arc<Mutex<T>>, first get the Mutex back with Arc::into_inner.

get_mut.title: How Mutex::get_mut works
get_mut.description: Direct &mut access when you own the Mutex exclusively.

slides.caption: &mut Mutex already proves nobody else is using it.
get_mut lends &mut 1.
It becomes 2.
Cheaper than lock() during setup.

is_poisoned.title: How Mutex::is_poisoned works
is_poisoned.description: true if a thread panicked while holding the lock.

slides.caption: A panic while locked "poisons" the Mutex, warning that the data might be inconsistent.
No panic so far: false.
A thread panicked holding the lock: true.
lock() then returns Err(PoisonError); into_inner() on that error still gives the data.

read.title: How RwLock::read works
read.description: Shared read access: many readers at once.

note.text: readers do not block each other

slides.caption: An RwLock allows many readers or one writer.
Reader 1 gets access.
Reader 2 too, at the same time.
Good for data that is read often and changed rarely, like configuration.

write.title: How RwLock::write works
write.description: Exclusive write access: waits until no readers or writers remain.

slides.caption: write() blocks new readers and waits for current ones to finish.
The write guard gives &mut access.
1 is pushed; the guard drops at the end of the line.
Holding a read guard and calling write() on the same thread deadlocks.

try_read.title: How RwLock::try_read works
try_read.description: Reads if possible right now; never waits.

slides.caption: Fails at once while a writer holds the lock.
No writer: Ok.
A write guard is alive: Err.
try_write is the writer version.

get_or_init.title: How OnceLock::get_or_init works
get_or_init.description: Initialises a value exactly once, even with many threads racing.

slides.caption: The first caller runs the closure; everyone else gets the same stored value.
A arrives first and initialises.
B gets the stored value; the closure never runs twice.
static CONFIG: OnceLock<Config> = OnceLock::new(); is the classic use.

set.title: How OnceLock::set works
set.description: Fills the OnceLock if empty; otherwise returns your value in Err.

slides.caption: Thread-safe write-once storage.
Empty: Ok.
Already set: Err(2).
get() returns Some only after a successful set.

force.title: How LazyLock works
force.description: A global value computed on first use, safely across threads.

slides.caption: Statics must be constant; LazyLock lets them hold computed values like a Vec or a HashMap.
The first access runs the closure.
Every later access, from any thread, sees the same Vec.
Replaces the older lazy_static! and once_cell crates.

call_once.title: How Once::call_once works
call_once.description: Runs a piece of code only the first time, no matter how often it is called.

slides.caption: Once remembers that it has run.
The first call runs the closure.
Later calls do nothing.
OnceLock is usually nicer, because it also stores a value.

wait.title: How Barrier::wait works
wait.description: Makes threads wait until all of them have arrived.

slides.caption: Each thread blocks in wait() until the third one arrives.
Threads 1 and 2 arrive and wait.
Thread 3 arrives: all three continue together.
Exactly one thread gets is_leader() == true, handy for one-time work after the barrier.

sync_channel.title: How mpsc::sync_channel works
sync_channel.description: A channel with a fixed capacity: send waits when it is full.

slides.caption: A bounded channel stops a fast producer from running far ahead of the consumer.
The first value fits.
The channel is full: send would wait, try_send fails.
sync_channel(0) makes every send wait for a matching recv (a rendezvous).

try_recv.title: How Receiver::try_recv works
try_recv.description: Takes a value if one is waiting; never blocks.

slides.caption: try_recv answers immediately.
Nothing sent yet: Empty.
A value is waiting: Ok(1).
Every Sender is dropped: Disconnected.
Good for game loops: handle all pending messages, then draw a frame.

recv_timeout.title: How Receiver::recv_timeout works
recv_timeout.description: Waits for a value, but only up to a time limit.

slides.caption: recv waits forever; recv_timeout gives up after the duration.
A value is ready: Ok(5).
Nothing within 10 ms: Timeout.
Lets a worker wake up regularly to check a stop flag.

try_iter.title: How Receiver::try_iter works
try_iter.description: An iterator over the values already waiting, without blocking.

slides.caption: try_iter stops as soon as the channel is empty, even if Senders still exist.
Three values are waiting.
They are collected; then it stops.
iter() would instead wait for more until every Sender is gone.
